definition: To work together with others to create or achieve something.
example: Nurses and doctors collaborate closely to plan each patient's recovery after surgery.
nuance: To collaborate is to share the work on a common product, while to cooperate can simply mean going along with others or not getting in the way.
prompt: Two students are assigned a joint science project about plant growth.
options: The partners agreed to collaborate, splitting the research and writing the report together.
Her lab notes collaborate his claim that the bean plant grew three inches in a week.
To collaborate on the poster, each partner secretly built a separate one and refused to share.
The teacher will collaborate the finished reports into one neat binder for the class.
reasons: Dividing tasks and producing one report as a pair is shared effort toward a common goal.
This confuses the word with corroborate, which means to confirm; notes cannot work with anyone.
Working in secret on separate posters is the opposite of joining forces.
This confuses the word with collate; gathering papers into order is not people working jointly.

practice.prompt: A poet and a guitarist meet to write a song for a school concert.
options: The poet will collaborate the short chorus with extra lines until it runs for six whole minutes.
The guitarist plans to collaborate with herself, writing all the words and music alone in her room.
The poet and the guitarist chose to collaborate, trading lines and chords until the song felt finished.
The poet refused to collaborate, so she and the guitarist wrote every verse side by side at one desk.
reasons: This confuses the word with elaborate, which means to add detail, not to work with a partner.
One person working alone has no partner, so no joint effort is taking place.
Exchanging ideas back and forth to build one song is two people creating something jointly.
Writing every verse together is teamwork, so saying she refused contradicts the rest of the sentence.
